Q: Prevent automatic storage of pseudo references A:

The two options I know of are:

  1. &&-qualifying all operations on pseudo-references.

    Then they can still be copied, but any use of the copy will error unless you std::move it (which should be enough to prevent accidental misuse).

  2. Making the pseudo-ref type non-copyable, and then doing this:

    Ref &&foo(int i, Ref &&ref = {})
{
    // Assign to `ref`.
    return std::move(ref);
}

    Since we now return an rvalue reference, copy elision doesn't apply.

    The temporary backing the reference lives to the end of the full expression as usual. (Note that if ref was passed by value, then the reference would dangle only on MSVC ABI, since elsewhere the parameters live until the end of the full expression.)

    The downside is making the API less clear. The user is never supposed to pass anything into ref, but it'll still appear in code completion.

Both options can be used at the same time.

Q: .NET 4.8 AllowAnonymous attrributes A:

The issue isn't the app per se, its IIS. [AllowAnonymous] by definition cannot let you bypass NLTM authentication.

There's two levels of authentication in .net framwork, your IIS (server) auth, and the ASP.NET (your app) auth.

IIS auth > ASP.net auth, it overrules what you're doing (IIS runs first, so if it rejects the request, your ASP.NET code never executes)

So what you need to do is override IIS authentication directly by doing this:

web.config file

<configuration>
  <location path="MyController/MyEndpoint">
    <system.webServer>
      <security>
        <authentication>
          <anonymousAuthentication enabled="true" />
          <windowsAuthentication enabled="false" />
        </authentication>
      </security>
    </system.webServer>
  </location>
</configuration>

all this means is that you're telling the server (IIS) that "for requests to 'MyController/MyEndpoint' please ignore Windows auth... allow anonymous access"

This is good when you want just that ONE endpoint public and everything else locked down

OR, you can do this: if you want the whole site's access control to be handled by the application instead of IIS, enable Anonymous Authentication at the site level in IIS:

  1. Open IIS Manager (inetmgr)

  2. Expand Sites → click your site (the one hosting this app)

  3. Open Authentication

  4. Set:

    • Anonymous Authentication → Enabled

    • Windows Authentication → Enabled (optional; keep it on if you still want Windows identity available)

  5. Restart the site or recycle the app pool (or run iisreset)

After that, requests will reach your ASP.NET pipeline, and then:

  • endpoints with [Authorize] will still require authentication

  • endpoints with [AllowAnonymous] will be accessible without authentication

Q: Unity Addressables for Android: Missing Textures with scene A:

Addressables are platform specific! Android indeed requires the shaders etc built differently so most probably since you load your Windows specific Addressables you run into Shader issues.

You will have to build Addressables once for Windows and also for Android and then for each according platform store them on your repository at different URL locations like e.g.

https://your.github.root.url/Addressables/Windows
https://your.github.root.url/Addressables/Android

Then accordingly also configure the remote source URL to the two different URL locations depending on the platform.

You do this in the Addressables Profile, either by having two of them according to your two (or more) target platforms (for full control over the URL format) - or even better for your use case at the bottom of that page (see section Adding a new variable and below) you will find how to configure dynamic variables for the URLs so you can use a single Profile but platform specific remote URL paths (in that case Unity directs how the exact URL needs to look like)

Q: How Do I Make a Calculator? A:

Start simple, don't try to build the whole thing at once.

since you already have csv files, first just focus on loading that data into Python using pandas or even just the built-in csv module. get comfortable reading and printing that data before anything else.

then think about the logic. fusion in persona games is basically just lookup tables right? persona A + persona B = persona C. so you are really just building a dictionary where two inputs return an output. strings all the way, no math needed.

something like:

fusion_table = { ("Pixie", "Slime"): "Ghoul" }

then you just take two user inputs, check if that combination exists in your table and return the result.

the tricky part is probably going to be loading your csv data into that dictionary structure cleanly. that's honestly where i'd spend most of your time figuring out.

if you get stuck, search specifically for "python dictionary lookup from csv" on stack overflow ,you will find exactly what you need without it being too advanced.

the fact that you already have the data in csv files is honestly half the battle. most people building something like this have to scrape the data themselves which is way more painful.
